objections.headline: Things we get asked.

items.q: Our staff won't switch to a new system.
items.a: Your staff isn't switching to a new way of working – they're doing the same things they've always done: creating appointments, confirming them, marking them done. The difference is it's now tracked instead of remembered. Most front-desk staff are comfortable within a day.

items.q: We have too many bookings to migrate.
items.a: Starting fresh doesn't mean losing history. Existing appointments stay where they are. You start using the platform for new bookings, and the value is immediate – without a migration project.

items.q: We already tried booking software before. It didn't stick.
items.a: Most booking tools are built for customers – not for the operational reality of a multi-branch team with managers, therapists, and admins. This one is built for how your business actually runs: with roles, branches, status flows, and a chain of accountability.

items.q: We're not sure we need all of this.
items.a: You don't need to use everything on day one. Most businesses start with booking creation and status management – and that alone changes how the morning works. Everything else is there when you're ready.

objections.sub: Answers to what owners ask before they switch.

objections.headline: Common questions.

items.q: We already track payments in another system.
items.a: If your current process doesn't connect payments to individual bookings, therapists, services, and branches in real time, you're only storing transactions. Zenly connects every payment to the work that generated it, giving you operational insight – not just accounting records.

items.q: What happens if a customer only pays part of the amount?
items.a: Partial payments are supported as part of the normal workflow. You can immediately see which bookings are fully settled and which still have an outstanding balance, making follow-ups simple and eliminating forgotten payments.

items.q: Will my staff have to do extra work?
items.a: No. Payment recording happens naturally as the booking is completed. Staff simply record the payment while closing the appointment, and everything else is updated automatically.

name: Staff Management

hero.headline: Your best therapist is needed at Branch 2 on Thursday. Everyone already knows.
hero.subheadline: Schedule staff moves between branches with an effective date. Assign therapists to bookings. Manage your team across every location without a single coordination call.
hero.imageAlt: Staff transfer and roster management screenshot

intro.headline: Schedule a staff transfer once. Everyone knows automatically.
intro.body: When a therapist needs to move branches, you schedule the transfer: who, where, and when the effective date is. The system updates. The destination branch sees the incoming staff member. The origin branch adjusts. No call. No message. No confusion on Thursday morning. And because every therapist is assigned to bookings by name, moving them between branches doesn't break existing appointments – it just re-anchors them at the right location.

_problem_hidden.headline: Multi-branch staff coordination is a full-time job you didn't sign up for.
_problem_hidden.body: You have a great therapist at your Thamel branch. But this week, the Lazimpat location is slammed and short-staffed. You want to move them over for three days. So you call the therapist. You call the Thamel manager to cover the gap. You call the Lazimpat manager to prepare. You update the schedule – on paper, or in a message thread, or in a mental note you'll forget by Wednesday. By Thursday morning, the therapist shows up at the wrong branch because someone's message got buried. A customer at Lazimpat waits. A customer at Thamel gets an apology. This is not a staffing problem. This is a coordination problem. And coordination problems have a system solution.

panels.title: Coordination via messages
panels.body: Staff assignments communicated in group chats, over calls, on sticky notes. Easy to miss. Impossible to reference. Gone the next time someone has a question.

panels.title: No forward planning
panels.body: You can react when someone is sick or a branch is overwhelmed. But you can't proactively plan therapist rotations, plan capacity, or build a schedule that holds across locations.

panels.title: Who works where today?
panels.body: The question no multi-branch owner should have to ask – but most do, every single morning.

name: Discount Management

hero.headline: Every discount your staff gives has a name attached to it. And an approval.
hero.subheadline: Stop finding out weeks later that your margins have been quietly disappearing. Every discount request is reviewed before it's applied — with a full record of who asked, why, and what was approved.
hero.cta: See how it works — book a 20-minute demo →
hero.trustLine: Across active branches, roughly 1 in 3 appointments carries a discount. Now every one of them is controlled.

intro.headline: Every discount starts with a request. Every request gets a decision.
intro.body: When a staff member wants to apply a discount, they submit a request — the percentage, the booking, the context. A manager reviews it. If it's approved, it goes through. If not, it doesn't. Simple. Structured. Logged. And because every applied discount is tied to a booking, a staff member, a service, and a value in NPR — you have a full audit trail. Not just for compliance. For understanding where your margins actually go.

_problem_hidden.headline: The most expensive word in a service business is "fine, just give them a discount."
_problem_hidden.body: It happens at the front desk, during checkout, in the middle of a complaint. A customer is unhappy. The appointment ran long. The staff member wants to smooth things over. So they offer 20% off. And they do it again tomorrow. And the day after. No one tracks it. No manager approves it. No report flags it. By the time you notice, you've given away thousands of rupees in margin that you'll never recover — to customers who may not even have deserved it. Discounting isn't the problem. Uncontrolled discounting is.

panels.title: Discounts as a habit, not a tool
panels.body: When staff can apply any discount at any time, it stops being a customer retention tool and starts being a reflex. "10% off" becomes the default response to every complaint, every delay, every awkward checkout moment.

panels.title: Margin erosion you can't see
panels.body: You won't find a line item called "discounts given without approval" in your weekly numbers. It hides inside revenue. You see lower totals. You assume it's a slow week.

panels.title: No accountability, no pattern
panels.body: Without a request record, you can't see which staff members discount most, which services get discounted most, or which branches are most exposed. You're managing blind.

name: Role-Based Access

hero.headline: Your staff see their schedule. Your managers see their branch. You see everything.
hero.subheadline: A three-tier access model built around how a real service business is structured — so every person has exactly the information they need, and no more than they should.
hero.cta: See role-based access in a 20-minute demo →

intro.headline: Three roles. Three views. One system — with the right boundaries.
intro.body: Every person in your business logs into the same platform. But what they see, what they can do, and what requires their approval is determined by their role — from front-desk staff to branch managers to the admin who sees it all.

_problem_hidden.headline: Giving everyone the same access sounds generous. It's actually a liability.
_problem_hidden.body: In most businesses that share software, everyone gets the same login. The owner, the manager, the person who started last week — same view, same permissions, same ability to change, delete, or override. It works until it doesn't. A staff member cancels a booking they shouldn't have. A manager adjusts pricing for a reason that isn't documented. A discount is applied directly, bypassing review. And because everyone had access to everything, you don't know who did what. Access without accountability isn't freedom. It's risk.

panels.title: Everyone can do everything
panels.body: When there are no role-based limits, every mistake is possible. A new staff member can accidentally change a booking that a manager just confirmed. There's no structural protection.

panels.title: No audit trail by role
panels.body: When something goes wrong, you have a list of events — but no clarity on who at what level was responsible. Accountability is impossible without role-based ownership.

panels.title: Sensitive information visible to everyone
panels.body: Revenue data, cross-branch performance, discount approval records — information that an owner or admin should own can end up visible to front-desk staff who have no context for what they're seeing.
